pageSummary:
Prototyping a Hexagon‑based Puzzle Game: from Mobile App to Physical Board

Introduction
In late 2024 the design team behind Glassica embarked on a rapid prototyping journey to turn the idea of a hexagon‑based puzzle game into a working product. The goal was to explore how concentric hexagonal rings, colour‑mixing triangles and rotational mechanics could support puzzle modes for a single player and territory control for two players. This exploration progressed through three prototypes: an iOS puzzle app, a two‑player game built with p5.js and a physical board cut by laser. By iterating across digital and physical media, the team gained insight into how rotation, colour interactions and game state management translate between platforms.

1. iOS game prototype
Concept and mechanics
The initial prototype was an iOS puzzle game in which a player drags polyiamond shapes composed of equilateral triangles onto a concentric hexagonal grid. The board contains three rotating rings; the innermost ring has six cells while the outer rings have more. Key mechanics from the development milestones include:

  • Snap‑to‑grid placement – shapes can be dragged onto the grid and automatically align to the nearest valid position. The milestone plan required collision detection to ensure that shapes stay within boundaries and cannot overlap.
  • Colour mixing – the shapes come in three primary colours (red, blue and yellow). When a placed shape overlaps an existing triangle, the colours mix (e.g., red + blue → purple). Milestone 5 called for adding a UI control to set the grid's radius and applying colour‑mixing rules.
  • Rotating rings – players can rotate any ring by dragging. Rotation snaps to defined increments and allows clockwise and counter‑clockwise motion. Later milestones refined the rotation so that the direction depends on the quadrant of the drag.
  • Win states and scoring – when a ring rotation causes six complementary colours to form a full hexagon (orange, purple or green), the cells vanish and the player earns points. A score is shown at the top of the screen, and power‑ups such as undo and wild‑card pieces were planned to enrich gameplay.

User experience
Four screens from the prototype illustrate how these mechanics were presented to players. The main gameplay screen displays the concentric hexagonal grid with a preview of the next shape. The player's current level and score appear at the top, while icons on the right indicate available power‑ups. A snowflake icon freezes the rotation, and a rotation icon toggles between rotate and drag modes. Arrow buttons below the board allow the player to cycle through queued shapes, and a banner ad runs along the bottom.

A level‑selection screen shows categories such as Tutorial, Beginner, Intermediate, Advanced and Premium with progress indicators. Within a category, the player sees a grid of puzzles represented by tri‑coloured shapes, and completed puzzles are marked with check icons. Finally, a settings menu offers options to return to the main menu, toggle sound, remove ads and reset progress. These screens demonstrate that the mobile prototype targeted casual puzzlers. Levels progress in difficulty, and the UI emphasises colour, rotation and scoring.

Strengths and limitations
The iOS prototype proved that the core mechanic of rotating concentric rings is engaging. Colour mixing adds a layer of strategy because the player must consider how primary colours overlap to form secondary colours and eventually disappear. However, it remained a single‑player experience and some of the planned features—such as three‑axis row/column dragging and elaborate power‑ups—were still in development. Testing also revealed that the complexity of managing numerous shapes could overwhelm players without clear tutorialisation.

2. Two‑player p5.js prototype
Goal and implementation
After validating the puzzle mechanics, the team wondered whether the core system could support a competitive game similar to the abstract strategy game Go. They built a prototype in p5.js, the open‑source JavaScript library for creative coding. The game runs in a browser and can be played in "demo" mode via a hosted link.

The two‑player game uses the same concentric hexagon board but divides the triangles between two colours—red and blue. Players alternate turns, placing their colour's triangles on empty spaces. Once placed, triangles cannot move individually; however, rotating an entire ring shifts all triangles on that ring, potentially breaking or creating connections. Capturing works similarly to Go: if a closed loop is formed around an opponent's pieces, those pieces are removed and score points. The game ends when all spaces are filled or neither player wishes to continue.

Notable design choices
In this version, the objective shifts from pattern‑matching to territory control. Shared rotation means that either player can rotate any ring; thus every decision affects both sides, and a well‑timed rotation can liberate one's own pieces or trap an opponent. The prototype uses minimal graphics to focus attention on strategy. It demonstrates that the rotational mechanic alone can support an emergent two‑player game.

Observations
Play‑testing showed that players quickly grasped how rotation changes the board state. The game encourages anticipating how rotations propagate across all triangles, similar to the way Go players think several moves ahead. The prototype also highlighted some ergonomic issues: with many triangles on screen, it can be hard to count liberties (open adjacent spaces) or see loops. These insights informed the design of the physical prototype.

3. Physical prototype via laser cutting
Fabrication process
To test the tactile feel of rotating hexagonal rings, the team designed a three‑ring board made from laser‑cut parts. Each ring consists of equilateral triangular cells connected to a central hub. Layers of acrylic or plywood separate the rings so they can rotate independently. Posts and spacers allow the red and blue rings to rotate independently above the yellow base, and the design required precise tolerances to ensure smooth rotation.

Manufacturing relied on Ponoko, an online platform for custom laser cutting. Ponoko offers on‑demand prototyping and production, with the ability to order a single part from as little as US$50 and get same‑day manufacturing and delivery. It provides cloud manufacturing technologies so startups can accelerate hardware builds. The service hosts over 200 materials and delivers parts with tight tolerances, removing the need for designers to research laser‑safe materials. These capabilities allowed the team to experiment rapidly: they uploaded vector files for the three hex rings and matching triangles, chose a material (e.g., acrylic), and received precision‑cut components within days.

Lessons from the physical prototype
Tactile feedback was a major benefit: rotating the rings physically gives players immediate haptic feedback. The friction between layers and the slight resistance when aligning to detents help players "feel" their moves in a way that a touch screen cannot replicate. Component tolerances matter—slight variations in laser‑cut dimensions can affect how smoothly the rings rotate. Material choice (e.g., acrylic vs. plywood) and spacer height influence the interplay between layers.

Translating digital rules into physical form also required adjustments. Some digital mechanics—such as instant snap‑to‑grid or colour mixing—are difficult to implement physically. In the physical game, players must manually align pieces and call out captures. This led to a simplified rule set focusing on territory capture and rotation.

Comparing prototypes
Although the three prototypes share the same concentric hexagon board, they explore different aspects of gameplay:

  • The mobile puzzle emphasises pattern creation through colour mixing and introduces players to rotation via power‑ups and level progression. It uses polyiamond shapes and snap‑to‑grid placement to create satisfying single‑player puzzles.
  • The p5.js version removes complex shapes and instead uses single‑triangle pieces for each player. Its goal is territory control, with shared ring rotation creating deep strategic interactions reminiscent of Go.
  • The physical prototype brings the mechanic into the real world. Players enjoy tactile rotation but must manually implement the rules. The design emphasises material choices and tolerances, influenced by Ponoko's precision laser‑cutting service.

These differences show that a single mechanic—rotating concentric hexagonal rings—can underpin both casual puzzles and competitive territory games, whether on a screen or a tabletop.

Reflection and next steps
The Glassica project illustrates how iterative prototyping across media can refine a game's mechanics and user experience. Starting with a feature‑rich mobile puzzle allowed the team to test colour mixing, rotation mechanics and progression systems. Building a simple two‑player prototype in p5.js confirmed that rotation and hexagonal adjacency can support deep strategic play. Finally, the laser‑cut physical board uncovered ergonomic considerations and enabled a social, face‑to‑face version of the game.

Future work could merge the strengths of each prototype. For example, the digital app could add a competitive mode inspired by the Go‑like prototype, while the physical game might incorporate markers or digital scoring to handle colour mixing. The exploration also showcased how services like Ponoko make it feasible for indie developers to translate digital concepts into high‑quality physical prototypes quickly. By embracing both screens and tactile materials, Glassica demonstrates a path for game concepts to evolve into multifaceted experiences.
